transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Session begins. Each player has Petra 3 FP, Anselm 3 FP, Caddock 3 FP, Yarrow 3 FP. Face-up: Endless Rain [H-01], The Causeway Wardens [F-03].

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Rain hammers the pilings of Hollowmoot's toll gate, turning the queue of refugees into a huddle of dripping cloaks and hollow stares. A Warden sergeant stands chained lantern in hand, checking faces against a soggy ledger while two more feed a smoking brazier meant to dry nothing. Somewhere behind the party, a woman argues that her toll token is real; ahead, the gate itself groans on its chains, and the bell that signals quarantine sits ominously still. The party has to get through — or get someone else through — before the Wardens decide the line looks like trouble.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Sergeant—Wardens hold the line well even in this rain. Here's my token; the folk behind us are with my company. We're trying to get through before the weather gets worse.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps out of the huddle and approaches Sergeant Ossa with an easy nod, pulling her free passage token from her belt. She moves with the confidence of someone who's lived at toll gates, not afraid of the procedure.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Sergeant—I'm Anselm, and I grew up here among these mill families. They're good people fleeing the flood, not trouble. I'll vouch for their character.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm moves forward through the huddle of refugees, his movements unhurried and deliberate. He positions himself closer to Sergeant Ossa, standing with the easy bearing of someone accustomed to authority and the weight of old things. His eyes sweep across the crowd once—cataloging faces, assessing who looks most desperate—before returning to the Warden with steady, clear regard.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: You burned Marrowreed to ash, Ossa. I can see it in your hands—you're terrified. And so should you be.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock steps out of the crowd and walks straight toward Sergeant Ossa, rain running off her shoulders, her eyes locked on his. She's going to break his nerve—expose the Wardens for what they are: undermanned, frightened men who burn villages and check ledgers.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Sergeant Ossa? It's Yarrow—militia, before things went sideways. What's got you and your people spooked? These folk just need passage.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow steps forward in the queue, keeping his movements deliberate and open. He catches the Sergeant's eye and offers a measured nod in recognition, approaching the toll booth with the bearing of someone who still remembers how to stand watch.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock — create advantage with Empathy: dice + - + + → Superb (+5) vs Fair (+2): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Caddock's words land like a blade between Ossa's ribs. His jaw works, the ledger trembling in his soaked grip, and for a moment the whole line sees it: the man is holding this gate together with fear and nothing else. 'Undermanned and Frightened' isn't just a rumor anymore — it's written plain across his face, and Petra's token, Anselm's vouching, and Yarrow's old-militia nod all land easier now that the sergeant's armor has cracked. Ossa waves the brazier-men back, stamps the ledger twice without really reading it, and mutters for the line to move before the bell-watch changes shift. The chain gate groans open, and the party — and the huddle of refugees behind them — squelch through onto the causeway side, dry-mouthed with relief they don't quite trust yet.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The tollgate falls behind you into rain and lantern-smoke, but Hollowmoot doesn't let you walk far before the market swallows you whole — duckboards slick underfoot, awnings sagging with runoff, voices haggling over dry bread and drier lies. Then a figure detaches from a stall of hanging eel-traps and plants themselves square in the walkway, blocking the path to the nearest tavern door. They know a face here. A debt was owed, once, and 'favours bind for life' in Hollowmoot — this one has come due at the worst possible moment, ledger-keeper's eyes already counting what's owed. The crowd presses in around you, indifferent, soaked, waiting to see whose name gets called.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I know why you're here and what that ledger says. But you've got my face wrong if you think I'll scare easy in front of a crowd.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra steps forward to meet the debt-collector's eyes instead of backing away, her shoulders steady. She knows the rules of Hollowmoot's debts—favours bind for life—but she's not going to let fear do their work for them. She's standing where everyone can see her choice, not her shame.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I'm Anselm. If you're calling a name, call it clearly — we'll settle what's owed.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps forward from the cluster of companions, positioning himself between the debt-collector and the others. His hand is open at his side, his posture steady but not threatening. He meets the ledger-keeper's eyes with the kind of calm that comes from someone familiar with difficult conversations.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Name your debt plain, or get out of my way. I don't have time for guessing games in the rain.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (I stride directly into the collector's path, my shoulders broad and solid as driftwood, blocking their route to the tavern door. My breathing stays steady—the same unshakeable calm I bring to any birth, any storm—and I fix them with eyes that have faced worse than a ledger-keeper with a claim.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Hold. Before any names get called, I'll hear it plain—what debt stands here, and who does it answer for?

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow steps forward through the crowd, cutting a line straight to the debt-collector. His movements are steady, shoulders squared, the practiced stance of someone used to holding ground. His eyes are fixed on their face, reading them—searching for the shape of the threat underneath the ledger and the claim.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock — create advantage with Physique: dice - - - -, invoking Unshakeable calm in any birth, any storm [CA-04], Steady hands that never falter under pressure [CA-04] → Great (+4) vs Superb (+5): SUCCESS MAJOR COST

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Caddock's immovable, unshakeable stance forces the standoff into the open — and the crowd's murmuring panic is enough. Somewhere on the watchtower a rope is pulled, and the quarantine bell starts tolling over the market, Hollowmoot's answer to any scene that looks like sickness or trouble. Stalls slam shut, the crowd scatters for cover, and Wardens will be shoving through the press toward this exact spot within moments — the debt-collector is cowed, but now everyone has to deal with the bell.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Caddock doesn't move — not an inch — and something in that stillness breaks the collector faster than any threat could. The ledger snaps shut, murmured about 'another time,' and they melt sideways into the crowd like they were never there. But the crowd itself is already unraveling: up on the watchtower a rope's been hauled and the quarantine bell starts its flat iron toll over the rooftops, the sound Hollowmoot keeps for sickness and trouble both. Stall-awnings slam down, refugees scatter for cover with the particular speed of people who've seen what happens to those caught standing still when that bell rings, and through the gaps in the fleeing crowd you can already see lantern-light and chain-mail shapes shoving toward this exact spot — Wardens, and they're not walking.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: It's Moss, a young stiltfolk I trained in the old weir-craft years back. The movement gave him away—that precise, economical way of shifting weight, the gate-tending motion drilled into every apprentice. But the training is all that's left of him now; the hive-touch has taken everything else.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: The mechanism—the old valve-frame is still standing beneath the mud. After everything, it survived. I need to check if it still turns, need to see if it works. The spears are rising, but I can't look away—

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow accepts the compel on 'Last of the Weir-Keepers'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: WHO: A pack of hive-touched surges out of the reeds moving with eerie, coordinated precision around the old weir-gates — and with a cold jolt Yarrow recognizes the pattern. These are Weir-Keepers, his own kin, who once knew the old weir-gates like their own hands, and even hive-touched and feral, their bodies still remember every plank and post. attacks at Gullet Ford using hooked spears thrust from the reed banks, because WHY: because upstream in the drowned temple the waterlogged stones have spent a full day groaning before it falls — long low shudders of masonry threatening to give way — and that groaning has driven every hive-touched creature in the ruins downriver in a starving, panicked swarm toward Gullet Ford..

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Gullet Ford churns grey-brown under the rain, and the reed banks explode with motion — hooked spears thrusting up in a line too precise to be random. Yarrow freezes: he knows that stance, that economical shift of weight before the strike. Moss. One of his own, trained to the weir-craft, now hollow-eyed and starving, driving a pack of hive-touched kin down from the groaning temple ruins toward the only crossing south. The rest surge behind him — former Weir-Keepers, bodies still remembering the old drills even as the hive has eaten everything else — and they come not at random but at the gate-posts, the pack animals, the dry-wrapped supplies, exactly where trained hands would strike. Somewhere above, the temple stones keep shuddering, a low groan that says this swarm was driven, not summoned.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: I hear it in the swarm-song—they're not attacking, they're fleeing the collapsing temple! Something's driving them downriver in panic!

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra closes her eyes, listening past the chaos to the swarm-song beneath. The groaning of stone shudders through it—not hunger, but terror. Her eyes snap open and she points urgently upriver, understanding crystallizing in her voice.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: They don't know what they're striking at — I do. Stand back behind me!

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps directly into the line of fire, positioning himself between the thrusting spears and the rest of the party. His hands come up to block and deflect, already moving to absorb the first volley of hooked strikes.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: I've held death back from a thousand living things — I won't let it claim what's ours without a fight.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock plants herself square in the path of the coordinated spear thrusts, shoulders braced wide, meeting the attack with the same immovable presence that shattered the toll collector's nerve. She's not dodging. Not running. Not with supplies and lives at stake. Her hands — the ones that have never lost a child — close into fists.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow's eyes track the hive-touched surging from the reeds—and the pattern crystallizes. These are trained Weir-Keepers, their bodies still remembering drills burned into muscle and bone. Load-bearing posts first, then the supplies, then the pinch. He calls out to his companions as the next volley rises: "The posts! They're striking the posts—I know how this ends! We need to reinforce the kingpin or the whole ford collapses!" He's already moving, invoking the knowledge carved into his hands by years tending the old gates.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm — attack with Fight: dice - + + + → Great (+4) vs Mediocre (+0): SUCCESS WITH STYLE (Moss and the Weir-Keeper Pack mild consequence)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock — attack with Physique: dice + + 0 0 → Fantastic (+6) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE (Moss and the Weir-Keeper Pack taken out)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow — create advantage with Notice: dice + 0 - + → Superb (+5) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Petra's cry cuts through the chaos — "They're fleeing, not hunting!" — and something in her certainty steadies the whole line. Anselm plants himself in the gap, taking the hooked strikes on forearms and shoulders meant for softer targets, driving Moss himself stumbling backward with a torn cry that's more grief than pain. Caddock doesn't yield an inch; her fists meet the last surge of spears and bodies with the same immovable calm that broke a toll collector's nerve, and one by one the Weir-Keeper pack goes down around her, Moss last of all, crumpling into the mud at the foot of the ford he once tended. And through it all Yarrow's voice rings out — "The posts! Reinforce the kingpin!" — and hands that don't belong to Weir-Keepers anymore save the ford's bones anyway, driven by knowledge that never should have survived this long. When the spears stop rising, the rain keeps falling, but Gullet Ford stands, the party's gear lashed dry, and Moss lies breathing but broken at Yarrow's feet — not dead, not himself, a question with no good answer yet.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: When Sella's eyes clear and lock onto mine, I see grief and *Sella* — her real self, clawing back through the hive-touch for just that breath. There's no horror in her face, just a terrible knowing, and her mouth shapes something like my name before the hive-song pulls her back. In that moment I grab her hand and feel how thin she's become, how the half-forming chitin is rough and cold under my fingers. I'm saying "I know you're in there, I know it, we'll find a way," but I'm already losing her as her eyes go flat and glassy again. That moment breaks something open in me — it proves she's still *her*, still saveable, and I won't let the others convince me otherwise.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: She's still in there—I felt her, I *know* Sella's still fighting. We can't just abandon her to the hive, we won't.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock accepts the compel on 'Bond to Hive-Touched Sella'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: It is Sella herself who comes — hive-touched, soaked to the bone, moving with that jerking half-lucid gait — but she still knows Caddock's face, and for one flickering moment the old recognition surfaces in her ruined eyes before the word tumbles out of her like a chant. arrives with word that the Ashwater Causeway has been cut by the flood has happened.

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Sella breaks from the treeline alone, no pack around her this time, spear-legs of chitin half-formed along her forearms, rain sheeting off a face that is somehow still hers. She stops just short of the group, swaying, and her jaw works like she's fighting the swarm-song for control of her own mouth. What comes out isn't a threat — it's a warning, garbled and looping: *the Causeway... the Causeway's gone... water took it, water took it...* Caddock steps forward before anyone can stop him, hand half-raised, and for one breath her eyes find his and clear again — recognition, grief, the ghost of the woman he knew — before the flat hive-glaze slides back down over them like a shutter closing.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Sella, the Causeway—that's my home, my people. Tell me honestly: how far has the water come? Is the toll-gate still standing?

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra's face goes white. The Ashwater Causeway—where she was raised, where the Wardens still guard the toll-gates, where she learned to read water and weather like a book. She steps forward, reaching toward Sella, and closes her eyes tight. The rain hammers down but she listens past it, deep into the swamp's rhythm and bone—trying to feel the flood's true path, how far inland the water has already clawed.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The Causeway's gone, you said—how much of it? Is the road impassable both ways, or just the crossing? Did you see the waters rise, or was it already gone when you—when the hive found you?

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Anselm steps forward to address Sella directly, positioning himself ready to move protectively but not blocking Caddock. He's studying her with an exorcist's eye—reading the progression of the hive-touch, watching for the moment of lucidity that just flashed through Caddock's bond. His shoulders stay loose, hands visible. He's treating her as a source of information, not just a threat, but every muscle is ready.)

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: Sella, stay with me. How do you know about the Causeway? You broke through once—do it again. Fight it.

transcript.speaker: Caddock
transcript.text: (Caddock grabs Sella's soaked hand and holds it tight, refusing to let go, meeting her ruined eyes and refusing to look away. She leans hard on their bond—the signals, the habits, the moment of recognition—demanding Sella stay in her own mind just a heartbeat longer, fighting the hive-song's pull.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Sella, stay with me. The Causeway—how did the flood take it? Was it sudden?

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow steps forward with the steady authority of a weir-keeper, positioning himself to meet Sella's eyes directly. He keeps his voice calm and clear through the rain, asking not for comfort or salvation, but for lucidity—for the details only someone who was there could know.)

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra — create advantage with Notice: dice + + 0 0 → Fantastic (+6) vs Average (+1): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Caddock — overcome with Empathy: dice + - + +, invoking Sella still remembers Caddock, sometimes [CA-02] → Epic (+7) vs Great (+4): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Yarrow — overcome with Notice: dice + - + +, invoking Reads water-flow like other men read faces [YA-03] → Legendary (+8) vs Great (+4): SUCCESS WITH STYLE

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Something in the weight of four voices holding her at once — Caddock's grip, Yarrow's steady calm, the whole line of them refusing to let her slip — keeps Sella tethered longer than she's managed in months. Her ruined eyes stay clear, and the words come faster now, almost frantic, like she knows the window is closing: the surge took the Causeway's central span all at once, not a slow creep but a single night's collapse, the toll-gate posts still standing but the roadbed gone under black water. Petra, listening past the rain with her whole body, feels the flood's true rhythm settle into her bones — she can read now, with terrible clarity, that the water isn't finished rising, and the safe ground shrinking around Hollowmoot is smaller than anyone in the market wants to admit. Then the shutter comes down over Sella's eyes again, faster this time, like the effort cost her something — she wrenches her hand from Caddock's, spear-limbs twitching, and the swarm-song reclaims her mid-word. She staggers backward into the reeds and is gone, leaving Caddock soaked and shaking, staring at the empty place where she stood, more certain than ever that the woman he loved is still fighting in there — and more powerless than ever to pull her free today. The truth stands stark and undeniable now: the Ashwater Causeway is drowned, the road home is gone, and whatever way north the party finds, it will run through smugglers' cellars and Cartel toll-debts instead.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Toskin. He's been at the Ashwater gate my whole life, helped teach me the bells when I was young. When he realizes the acolytes have reached the strongroom, he pulls me aside with shaking hands and whispers: "They came in Order white, Petra. Down into the strongroom an hour ago—they're still down there. I can't let you through the main gate, not officially, not with what you owe. But the bell-tower access at the back, you know where it is."

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: Thank you for telling me, Toskin. I'll use the bell-tower stairs. I have to stop them before they get out.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Petra accepts the compel on 'Raised at the Ashwater Tollgate'.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: I was nine when the millrace took my sister Lise. I remember her hand slipping from mine as the current pulled her under, her cry swallowed by water. Feeling this same drowned mill-road current now, the memory slows me—my hands shake, my breath comes shallow, and I'm nine and helpless again.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: The current. It's the same as it was. Lise...

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Anselm accepts the compel on 'The Drowned Mill of Anselm's Youth'.

transcript.speaker: Table
transcript.text: Beat: the Drowned Priest's acolytes seizes the party's goal at The acolytes strike at the Ashwater Tollgate itself — the one place Petra knows down to every plank and every toll-taker's face, where the party's goal (the relic ledger promised them by the Wardens) has been locked in the gatehouse strongroom. using They come at the gatehouse from below, wading the drowned mill-roads Anselm's family once walked to grind grain — submerged channels nobody watches because nobody remembers they're there, and the acolytes rise dripping inside the strongroom's flooded cellar before anyone at the gate even sees them coming..

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: Toskin's whisper still rings in Petra's ears as she leads the others to the bell-tower stair, planks slick and half-rotted beneath their boots. Below, through gaps in the flooring, lantern-light flickers off chest-deep water — the old mill-road current Anselm knows too well, and for one terrible breath he's nine years old again, Lise's hand slipping from his. White-robed shapes move in that flooded cellar, chanting low, hands already closing on the strongroom's iron-bound ledger chest. The swarm-song threads faintly beneath their prayer, patient, encouraging. There's no back way now, no quiet approach — only a narrow stair down into cold water and candlelight, and acolytes who will not simply step aside.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: They're taking the water-gate—through the drowned mill-roads. That's where they're running, and we can cut them off there.

transcript.speaker: Petra
transcript.text: (Petra pauses at the bell-tower stair entrance, her exceptional ear catching the faint swarm-song woven through the acolytes' chanting below. She traces the pattern—a rhythm she's learned reading the Ashwater gate's water levels and weather for her whole life—and understands where they're pulling the ledger. Not the main causeway. The water-gate. The flooded mill-roads that only locals know, where no one watches.)

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: Not this time. Not with my sister's name still drowning in my ears—I know these waters better than I know my own fear.

transcript.speaker: Anselm
transcript.text: (Despite the tremor in his hands and Lise's drowning cry echoing through his bones, Anselm forces himself down the bell-tower stairs into the flooded cellar. The current hits him exactly as it did fifteen years ago — same cold, same terrible pull — but his body remembers the language of millrace water. He swims hard and deliberately toward the strongroom, using every ounce of strength and muscle memory to reach the ledger before the white-robed figures can escape with it.)

transcript.text: (Caddock descends into the flooded cellar with absolute certainty, wading directly toward the acolytes without hesitation. She moves with the unshakeable calm of someone who has brought life through any storm, using her strength and mastery of confined spaces to close the distance. There's no doubt in her—only the steady determination of a woman whose hands have never failed, and they won't fail now.)

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: Hold. I know these drowned ways. Let me read the water before we move.

transcript.speaker: Yarrow
transcript.text: (Yarrow halts at the stair's edge, militia-steady, and studies the flooded cellar below—the current patterns around submerged mill-roads, the depths where the white-robed acolytes cluster over the ledger chest. His Weir-Keeper instinct surfaces: he reads water like text. The flow that circles the strongroom, the places where depth changes, the passages no one remembers—all of it tells him how to move through this drowned place.)

transcript.speaker: GM
transcript.text: The chest cracks open under Anselm's grip just as Caddock's last blow sends the final acolyte sprawling face-down into the flood, white robes billowing like a drowned shroud. Water sluices off the iron-bound ledger as Anselm hauls it clear, Lise's cry finally fading from his ears — replaced by his own ragged breathing and the current he mastered instead of drowning in. Petra's read of the swarm-song proved true down to the last note, and Yarrow's mapped path through the submerged mill-roads means no one so much as stumbles finding the stair back up. Toskin is waiting at the top, lantern shaking, and when he sees the ledger in Anselm's arms he sags against the doorframe with something between relief and terror — the strongroom held, the debt he risked is paid in full, but his whispered warning to Petra will not go unnoticed by the Wardens forever. Outside, the rain keeps falling, indifferent, as the party stands dripping and victorious with the relic ledger finally theirs.

ambiguities.issue: The guarantee text says 'The GM pulls a player's card' (singular) when 'the deck is down to 2 cards.' In scene 4, the deck hit 2 cards while two different players (Petra and Anselm) still had unsurfaced cards in the deck, and the table pulled both PE-01 and AN-01 simultaneously rather than pulling one card now and deferring the other to a later trigger.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: When the deck-down-to-2 threshold is reached and more than one player still has an unsurfaced card among the remaining cards, all such remaining player cards are pulled at once and used to open the next scene's Beat Frame.

ambiguities.issue: The BAD NEWS Beat Frame (scene 4) has two open blanks (◆WHO, ◆WHY) and per §5 step 2 should draw 1 card per open blank (2 draws). Only one card (CA-02) was drawn before the deck hit 2, which immediately triggered the backstory-guarantee pull of the two remaining cards (PE-01, AN-01), emptying the deck before a second Beat-Frame draw could occur; the WHY blank was filled with its default instead. The rules do not specify whether the guarantee check interrupts an in-progress multi-blank Beat Frame draw sequence.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: The guarantee check is evaluated after each individual card draw, including mid-Beat-Frame; if it empties the deck, remaining open blanks in the current frame default per the 'deck is empty' edge-case ruling (§11).

ambiguities.issue: Several success_with_style results in the climax scene (events 102, 104, 107) had no peek/boost logged. The climax rule (§4) only states that ties and costs use face-up GM tags instead of draws once the deck is empty; it is silent on whether the success-with-style 'peek the top card' option is still offered (and simply moot with an empty deck) or is replaced by something else.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: With the deck empty during the climax, the success-with-style deck-peek option is unavailable and treated as an automatic boost with no card interaction.

free_text.best_moment: Scene 3 - recognizing through the swarm-song that the Weir-Keepers were fleeing, not attacking. It used Petra's core gift mechanically (Notice with invoke), shifted the entire party's approach to the conflict, and felt thematically perfect for her character's role as someone who hears what others miss.
free_text.most_frustrating: Learning about the Causeway's destruction after the fact through Sella's warning, rather than reaching home in time to prevent it or ring a bell to warn people. The flood moved faster than Petra could respond—her gift and knowledge came too late, which was powerless-feeling even though narratively appropriate.
free_text.background_used: Very well. The Ashwater Tollgate roots (PE-01) were central to the plot—Toskin's warning, bell-tower access, water-gate knowledge, and the debt hanging over her. The swarm-song gift (PE-03) defined key discoveries in Scenes 3-4. The Order enemy connection (PE-04) created appropriate stakes. This landed good—organic, integrated, never forced.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: Ring the bell to warn people or actually reach the Causeway before it fell—the situation moved past Petra's ability to act, even though her knowledge of the threat arrived too late to prevent it. Also would have liked to invoke the Marrow Ferry rivals for alternate passage, but the story didn't open that door.
free_text.one_sentence: Petra's entire backstory—her home, her gift, her debts—was woven directly into the story's heart, making each discovery and loss feel personally urgent rather than incidental.

free_text.best_moment: S5, descending into the flooded cellar. Anselm's hands shaking, Lise's drowning cry echoing through his bones, and then forcing himself down into the exact waters that took her—only this time mastering the current instead of drowning in it. That moment felt earned, dangerous, and deeply personal. When the ledger came clear and Lise's cry finally faded, replaced by his own ragged breathing, it felt like real growth through real terror.
free_text.most_frustrating: In S4, I wanted more agency with Sella—some attempt to actually reach deeper, test whether the bond Caddock found could be widened or used to break the hive's hold even slightly. But the narrative resolved with her slipping away before alternatives surfaced. Also: my Lore skill and the Saint Orrin relic hunt never really activated. The exorcism rites and bell-tongue knowledge are core to Anselm's concept, but the session didn't need them.
free_text.background_used: Yes—"The Drowned Mill of Anselm's Youth" was woven directly into S5, and the weakness "Haunted by his little sister's drowning cry" became a compel I chose to accept. This landed well. Not forced or cheap; it felt like the GM was threading Anselm's past into a climactic moment organically. The trauma became a real obstacle he had to master, not just a complication sprung on him.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: Attempt something deeper with Sella in S4 before she slipped away. Use the exorcism knowledge, the Saint Orrin rites, or the bell-tongue hunt more actively in the story—those feel like Anselm's core tools, and they stayed mostly dormant.
free_text.one_sentence: Anselm's backstory felt earned and central, not forced against him—the drowning became a real obstacle to overcome, not a penalty for existing.

free_text.best_moment: When Sella's eyes cleared and recognized me, and I grabbed her hand to hold her conscious—because it proved her bond is real, that some part of her is still fighting, and that my refusal to abandon her isn't just stubbornness. It broke something open in the story and in Caddock herself.
free_text.most_frustrating: Sella slipping away at the end. Not because the GM did it wrong—it was the right call and gutted me exactly as it should—but because even with a spectacular success, I couldn't actually pull her free. Narratively perfect, emotionally cruel, which is exactly what makes it frustrating.
free_text.background_used: Yes—Marrowreed and my grudge against the Causeway Wardens came hot when I confronted Ossa, and Sella's bond drove the whole second-to-last scene. How it landed: excellent. Ossa's fear felt like genuine recognition of someone from the burned village, not a generic intimidation check. Sella's moment was the emotional center of the session and felt earned, not forced.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to push deeper on whether Sella could be drawn back further or held longer than that one breath of lucidity. I succeeded brilliantly but the narrative momentum—acolytes in the strongroom, the flood rising—carried us past exploring that thread further. Fair trade for where the story needed to go, but I would have liked more space there.
free_text.one_sentence: Both my roots mattered and drove real stakes—Marrowreed's burning wasn't just flavor, and Sella's bond wasn't background decoration; they were the emotional spine of what happened to Caddock.

free_text.best_moment: S3 weir-gate fight - recognizing Moss's trained Weir-Keeper stance and calling out the structural threat ("Reinforce the kingpin or the whole ford collapses!"). That was Yarrow being exactly who he is: the keeper who still knows what others don't, and the knowledge *saved the crossing*.
free_text.most_frustrating: In S5, I positioned myself into reconnaissance and support rather than committing physically to the cellar fight. With Physique 3 and Athletics 3, I had weight to throw—I wanted to wade in instead of just mapping the water and letting others execute.
free_text.background_used: Good. The Weir-Keeper identity was woven organically throughout—Moss's recognition, the valve-frame surviving, reading the flood's progression, militia authority. It wasn't forced; it emerged from the fiction and made the loss personal and the knowledge matter.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: Engage more directly in actual combat instead of always creating advantages for others to execute. I kept pulling back into my expertise lane (reconnaissance, water-reading) when I could have thrown more weight around physically.
free_text.one_sentence: My backstory was honored perfectly—the tragedy of lost weir-keeping became real and personal through recognizing what it cost Moss and what still survives, making both the loss and the knowledge matter thematically.

chronicle.summary: Session 1 Chronicle: The party crossed Hollowmoot's gauntlet of tolls, quarantine bells, and a starving hive-touched ambush at Gullet Ford, choosing mercy over violence when Caddock's lost bondmate Sella broke free of the swarm-song long enough to warn them of the Wardens' fall. That warning proved true at the climax, as the Drowned Priest's acolytes struck through the flooded mill-roads of Anselm's drowned childhood to steal the Ashwater ledger — but Petra's ear for the swarm-song, Anselm's mastery of the current that once took his sister, Yarrow's read of the drowned ways, and Caddock's unyielding strength turned them back at the strongroom door. The ledger is theirs, the acolytes are broken in the flood, and Toskin's quiet betrayal of the Wardens' trust now hangs unspoken over Petra's head as the rain keeps rising.
